response.query: How should Delphi/AHP elicited weights be converted into Bayesian priors (parametric form, informative vs weakly informative choices) and how to report prior sensitivity?
response.answer: Convert Delphi/AHP weights into Bayesian priors by using them to define parameter distributions; choose informative or weakly informative priors based on available knowledge; report prior sensitivity through posterior distribution comparisons.

results.title: Informative Priors: Bayesian Statistics Essentials
results.content: Informative priors are a crucial component of Bayesian statistics, allowing researchers to incorporate prior knowledge into their models. * **Informative priors**: These are prior distributions that incorporate prior knowledge or information about the parameter. Prior elicitation is the process of determining the prior distribution based on prior knowledge or information. flowchart LR A["Define problem and parameter"] --> B["Elicit prior distribution"] B --> C["Specify prior distribution"] C --> D["Update prior with data"] D --> E["Analyze results"] E --> F["Validate results"] F --> G["Refine prior or model"]. The mathematical representation of informative priors involves specifying a prior distribution for the parameter of interest. By understanding the fundamentals of informative priors, eliciting and specifying prior distributions, and implementing them in practice, researchers can make more accurate predictions and better decisions. ### What are informative priors in Bayesian statistics? ### How are informative priors elicited? Some common challenges when working with informative priors include prior-data conflict, prior elicitation bias, and model misspecification.

results.title: A Bayesian Workflow Question: prior sensitivity with respect to observed data for complex models - Modeling - The Stan Forums
results.content: # A Bayesian Workflow Question: prior sensitivity with respect to observed data for complex models. However, I have a question about the emerging PBW (that’s principled Bayesian workflow, not Pabst Blue Workflow) that was motivated by a reviewers comment on a manuscript about whether a prior was truly weakly informative with respect to my observed data. The PBW address prior sensitivity through simulated data with question three. But my reviewer seems more concerned with assessing prior sensitivity with respected to my observed data. One option would be to choose some set of different priors and refit the model to see if the posterior predictive checks and posterior distributions change very much. So it isn’t clear how to do such a sensitivity analysis: do I change the priors for parameters one at time holding all others fixed? One thing I thought of would be to assess posterior shrinkage using the same measure as specified by @betanalpha in the workflow: s = 1 - \frac{\sigma^2\_{post}}{\sigma^2\_{prior}}s=1−σ2postσ2prior. Firstly in the context of the prior model *weakly informative* does not mean *non-informative*. A consequence of this is that there is no expectation that weakly informative priors will not influence posterior inferences. All a prior sensitivity analysis\* demonstrates is that your prior assumptions influence your inferences, but there’s nothing wrong with that influence! I don’t care if my weakly informative prior scales influence the posterior under a collinear likelihood function so long as we can all agree that those scales isolate extreme model configurations that would be unreasonable in the context of the given analysis. For example it can refer to how sensitive a decision making process is to the particular observed data (i.e. sampling observations and running the analysis over and over again to see the range out of outcomes), how sensitive inferences are to the experimental design (i.e. sampling observations from various data generating process, running the analysis over and over again, and seeing how the range out of outcomes varies with the underlying data generating process), and how sensitive inferences are to model assumptions (the approximations made in the observational model, the domain expertise encoded in the prior model, etc).

results.title: Should Bayesian inference be avoided with a small sample size and weakly informative priors? - Cross Validated
results.content: # Should Bayesian inference be avoided with a small sample size and weakly informative priors? Given this, if you know beforehand that your priors are weak *and* that you have a small sample size, should you avoid Bayesian inference? $\begingroup$ To the contrary, objective Bayesian priors have the effect of smoothing parameter estimates in small samples and can be helpful. With small n and no reliable prior, instead of a Bayesian analysis---or even a Frequentist analysis (which may just confirm that "The sample is too small to estimate these parameters with adequate precision")---I would just report descriptive statistics / graphs and be very transparent about the study's limitations: due to the sample size, our results cannot safely generalize to the population, etc. But if we can write down *several* extremely weak priors and we have too little knowledge to confidently choose one of them -- and our sample's so small that the posterior will be sensitive to our choice among these weak priors -- then probably we should indeed do descriptive work or theory instead of inference. 2") Bayesian design for a small sample and how to include informed priors.
